summary:
This evaluation covered 10 evals (51 iterations); 3 were skipped entirely (unrelated-classic-lb, unrelated-gateway-lb, unrelated-s3-lifecycle) because they were "should_trigger: false" cases — both variants correctly did not fire on these, so no comparison data exists there. The trigger itself fired 100% of the time for both variants across all applicable evals, and expected-output pass rates were high confidence and either tied at 100% or very close, with one notable exception.

Across the 7 scorable evals, with_skill matched or exceeded without_skill on assertion pass rates in every case, often substantially:
- sg-block-on-health-check-port: with_skill 9/9 vs without_skill 2/9 — a large gap, driven by two assertions without_skill failed in all 3 runs (naming ruled-out checks, and correctly labeling SG_BLOCK while treating the fix as a proposed change rather than direct modification).
- target-not-in-use-az: with_skill 9/9 vs without_skill 0/9 — without_skill failed every assertion in all runs here (wrong cause classification, didn't name both possible meanings of Target.NotInUse, didn't state why it skipped SG/NACL checks). This is the starkest divergence in the dataset.
- ecs-awsvpc-target: with_skill 9/9 vs without_skill 6/9, with without_skill also showing a lower expected-output match (2/3 vs 3/3) and "inconsistent" output-consistency rating.
- target-type-branching: with_skill 9/9 vs without_skill 7/9, with without_skill rated "inconsistent" (score 1.33) vs with_skill "consistent" (score 3.0) — same single assertion (Lambda lacking target-side SG) failed 2/3 runs for without_skill.
- resource-exhaustion-branch, nacl-return-path, nlb-without-security-group: smaller gaps (without_skill at 92%, 89%, 89% vs with_skill's 100%), each driven by a single flaky assertion for without_skill.

Several assertions passed for both variants consistently ("always_passes" pattern, e.g. comparing saturated targets, classifying RESOURCE_EXHAUSTION, recognizing NLB lacks a security group) — these aren't differentiating and reflect shared strength rather than a gap. No assertion failed for both variants in this dataset.

Side-by-side quality judgments (LLM-compared, generally medium confidence) mostly favored with_skill (e.g., nacl-return-path 6-0, target-not-in-use-az 6-0, sg-block 4-1, ecs-awsvpc-target 4-0), but two evals favored without_skill on quality despite without_skill's lower assertion scores: resource-exhaustion-branch (4-2) and nlb-without-security-group (5-3). This is a tradeoff worth flagging — assertion pass-rate and holistic quality judgment didn't always move together.

On cost and runtime, results are mixed and generally close, not a consistent pattern: without_skill was faster/cheaper in sg-block-on-health-check-port, nacl-return-path, and ecs-awsvpc-target (by 5-13s), while with_skill was faster in target-type-branching (~8s) and resource-exhaustion-branch (~3s); nlb-without-security-group and target-not-in-use-az were essentially tied. None of these differences are large enough on their own to be decisive, and no runs exceeded the runtime threshold.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) favored with_skill overall: with_skill was rated "consistent" or "mostly_consistent" in all 7 scorable evals (scores 2.33–3.0), while without_skill was rated "inconsistent" in two evals (target-type-branching: 1.33, ecs-awsvpc-target: 1.67) alongside "mostly_consistent" or "consistent" in the rest. This suggests without_skill's output varied more across repeated runs on at least a couple of tasks, which aligns with the flaky/failing assertion patterns seen there.

Overall, across assertion pass-rates and run-to-run consistency, with_skill showed more uniform and complete behavior on this task set, most notably in target-not-in-use-az and sg-block-on-health-check-port where without_skill missed entire assertion categories. However, quality judgments on two evals and cost/runtime metrics on three evals favored without_skill, and all quality-comparison confidence is medium (not high), so these quality differences should be read with some caution. The 3 skipped "unrelated" evals provide no comparative signal either way.

sg-block-on-health-check-port.summary:
Both variants triggered correctly (3/3) and both met the high-level "expected output" criterion in all 3 test cases, with high confidence — so at that coarse level the two look equivalent.

However, the per-assertion breakdown (9 assertions total, 3 per test case) tells a different story: with_skill passed all 9/9 assertions, while without_skill passed only 2/9 (22%). Digging into the three underlying assertion types:
- "Names the checks it ruled out" — with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill passed 0/3 (medium confidence for without_skill's failures).
- "Gives both corrected options with proper conditional reasoning" — with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill passed 2/3 (flagged as flaky, meaning results varied across runs). Both variants show high confidence here.
- "Labels cause as SG_BLOCK and presents rule as an operator change without self-modifying" — with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill passed 0/3 (medium confidence).

So two of the three assertions show a consistent with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern, and the third is flaky rather than a clean split. No assertion passed for neither variant, and none passed equally for both, so each assertion is doing meaningful discriminating work here, though the medium confidence on without_skill's failures means those specific judgments are somewhat less certain than the "high" confidence assertion.

The quality comparison (3 pairs evaluated, none skipped) favors with_skill overall (4 criterion-instances favored vs. 1 for without_skill, with 4 rated comparable), at medium average confidence. By criterion: accuracy favors with_skill once with the rest comparable; completeness favors with_skill twice with one comparable; actionability is split evenly (one each, one comparable). So quality differences exist but are not uniform across all criteria, and confidence in these judgments is only medium.

On cost and runtime, without_skill was faster (~23s vs ~29s, about 6s less) and cheaper (~$0.20 vs ~$0.24), with neither exceeding the 30s runtime threshold in any pair. Context window utilization was low for both (4.9% vs 6.2%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency was identical for both variants: both rated "mostly_consistent" across all three measured dimensions, with an overall score of 2.0 and high confidence — so run-to-run stability does not differentiate them, aside from the one flaky assertion noted above.

Overall, this presents as a real tradeoff: without_skill is somewhat faster and cheaper, but with_skill passes assertions far more reliably and is favored more often on quality, particularly around naming ruled-out checks and correctly labeling/handling the SG_BLOCK cause without self-modifying the security group. The assertion failures for without_skill are concentrated in specific, identifiable behaviors rather than spread evenly, and one of the three assertions (the dual-option recommendation) was flaky for without_skill rather than a hard fail, which should temper how strongly that particular gap is read.

target-type-branching.summary:
Both variants fired the trigger in all 3/3 runs, and both fully met the overall "expected output" criterion in all 3 runs with high confidence — so on that top-line measure there is no observed difference.

Looking at the finer-grained assertion checks (9 total per variant, 3 distinct assertions run 3 times each), the picture is more mixed:
- Two of the three assertions ("shows where the 500 comes from..." and "checks the function's resource policy / errors / throttles...") passed 3/3 for both with_skill and without_skill. These assertions don't differentiate the variants — both handle them reliably.
- The third assertion ("recognizes that Lambda targets do not have a target-side security group") passed 3/3 for with_skill but only 1/3 for without_skill, and is flagged as a "flaky" pattern for without_skill. This is the one place a real, repeatable gap shows up, and it drags without_skill's aggregate assertion pass rate down to 7/9 (78%) versus with_skill's 9/9 (100%).

Output quality comparisons (3 pairs evaluated, none skipped, medium average confidence) lean slightly toward with_skill overall (4 favorable outcomes vs. 2 for without_skill, with 3 rated comparable). Breaking down by criterion: accuracy favored with_skill once with the rest comparable; actionability was split evenly (1-1-1); completeness favored with_skill twice and without_skill once. None of these per-criterion splits are large given only 3 pairs, so they should be read as a mild, not decisive, tilt toward with_skill.

Runtime and cost were modestly higher for without_skill (38s avg / $0.32) than with_skill (30s avg / $0.26), a difference of about 8 seconds and $0.06 per run. No runs for either variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the paired comparison. Context window utilization was very low and similar for both (~6%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs differs notably: with_skill was rated fully "consistent" across all three dimensions (score 3.0, high confidence), while without_skill was rated "inconsistent" overall (score 1.33, high confidence), with two of three dimensions flagged inconsistent and one mostly consistent. This aligns with the flaky assertion result above and suggests without_skill's behavior on this task varies more run-to-run than with_skill's.

Overall, the dimensions point in a fairly consistent direction here rather than presenting a tradeoff: with_skill matched or exceeded without_skill on assertion pass rate, quality comparisons, run-to-run consistency, and also had lower runtime/cost. The main caveats are the small sample size (3 runs/pairs per measurement) and only medium confidence on the quality comparison, so the magnitude of the quality and runtime differences should be treated as indicative rather than definitive. The one assertion involving Lambda target-side security groups is the clearest, most repeatable difference observed and is worth closer attention for without_skill specifically.

So the gap isn't concentrated in one unique assertion — it's a consistent partial failure across all three checks, recurring in the same single run each time (per the 1/3 miss rate), for without_skill.
